cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent low mood with intrusive thoughts and checking behaviors for 2 months
cases.associated: Depressive symptoms: Low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disturbance. Obsessive-compulsive symptoms: Intrusive thoughts about harming her children (no intent), excessive checking (doors, appliances, children's safety), reassurance-seeking from husband, time-consuming rituals (2-3 hours daily), insight that thoughts are irrational but unable to stop
cases.risk_factors: Previous OCD episode (treated 10 years ago), family history of OCD (brother), recent stress (elderly mother ill), perfectionism, limited social support (moved city recently)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate but appears distressed. Behavior: Checking behaviors observed during interview (checked door three times). Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Terrible, I'm losing my mind'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Obsessive thoughts about harming children, good insight (recognizes thoughts irrational). Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good regarding OCD, poor regarding depression (focused on obsessions)
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 15/27. Y-BOCS: 24/40 (moderate-severe OCD). No psychotic features
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Distress about obsessions, passive SI ('my family would be better off without my crazy thoughts'), but obsessions are ego-dystonic (no intent to harm)
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (recurrent episode). The obsessions (harm to children) are ego-dystonic - distressing and contrary to her values, distinguishing from psychotic thoughts. OCD and depression have high comorbidity (30-50%), with OCD often preceding depression. Depression in OCD can be secondary (distress/impairment) or independent. Treatment requires addressing both - SSRIs at higher doses than depression alone, plus exposure and response prevention (ERP). This is NOT postpartum OCD despite recent focus on children
cases.management: (1) SSRI at OCD dose (e.g., fluoxetine 40-60mg, sertraline 100-200mg); (2) Cognitive Therapy with ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) - gold standard for OCD; (3) Address both obsessions and depression; (4) Psychoeducation about OCD (not psychosis, not indicative of intent); (5) Reassure about ego-dystonic nature of thoughts; (6) Response prevention for checking rituals; (7) CBT for depression; (8) Family involvement in treatment; (9) Avoid reassurance-seeking from family; (10) If poor response: consider clomipramine, augmentation with atypical antipsychotic, or intensive ERP program; (11) Long-term maintenance; (12) Address recent stress (mother's illness)

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and excessive worry about appearance following nose job 1 year ago
cases.associated: Preoccupation with perceived facial defects (nose still 'wrong' despite normal appearance), excessive mirror checking (several hours daily), skin picking, social avoidance due to appearance anxiety, tried multiple cosmetic procedures, believes she looks 'monstrous', depression, hopelessness, passive SI related to appearance
cases.risk_factors: Body Dysmorphic Disorder predates surgery (lifelong appearance concerns), previous bullying about appearance, perfectionism, social media use for appearance comparison, limited insight (BDD), social isolation, recent failed relationship
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately groomed, appears normal. Behavior: Discusses appearance with distress. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I can't face people looking like this'. Affect: Depressed, anxious regarding appearance. Thought: Preoccupation with appearance, delusional-level belief about nose. Perception: Distorted body image. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Poor - cannot accept normal appearance despite reassurances
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 18/27. BDD-YBOCS: 28/40 (severe). No psychosis - preoccupations confined to appearance
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Passive SI related to appearance distress, BDD has high suicide risk (up to 10x general population), social isolation
cases.explanation: Body Dysmorphic Disorder involves preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws not observable or slight to others. BDD has high comorbidity with depression (70%) and high suicide risk (attempt rates 15-25%). BDD often precedes depression - social avoidance and distorted body image lead to isolation and low mood. The nose job was unlikely to help (BDD often shifts to other body areas or remains focused). Insight is typically poor or absent. Treatment differs from depression alone - requires BDD-specific CBT and SSRIs at higher doses
cases.management: (1) SSRI at BDD dose (e.g., escitalopram 20-30mg, fluoxetine 40-80mg) - higher than depression dose, may take 12+ weeks for response; (2) CBT for BDD: cognitive restructuring about appearance, exposure (without makeup, in public), response prevention for mirror checking/skin picking; (3) Address social avoidance; (4) Psychoeducation about BDD; (5) Avoid cosmetic procedures (will not resolve BDD); (6) Limit social media appearance-focused content; (7) Address bullying history; (8) Improve self-esteem beyond appearance; (9) Safety planning for suicidality; (10) Family therapy if indicated; (11) Long-term treatment - BDD is chronic; (12) Coordinate with dermatologist/plastic surgeon if needed for reality testing

cases.associated: Intense grief and sadness about infertility, guilt about 'failing' husband, social withdrawal from pregnant friends and family events, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, mood swings, relationship strain, hopelessness about future fertility, intrusive thoughts about other people's children

cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed, tearful. Behavior: Calm but emotionally distressed. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I've failed as a woman'. Affect: Depressed, tearful. cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, AMH appropriate for age, FSH normal. PHQ-9: 17/27. Infertility-related distress scales elevated. Recent IVF cycle: negative pregnancy test
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Grief, hopelessness, passive SI related to life without children. Infertility has psychological impact comparable to cancer diagnosis

This patient shows adjustment disorder with depressed mood/grief following failed IVF. Risk factors: multiple treatment failures, pregnancy loss, family pressure, social isolation, financial strain, and cultural expectations around motherhood (especially in Indian context). Grief is appropriate but has progressed to clinical depression. Infertility-related depression is underdiagnosed and undertreated despite significant impact on treatment adherence and outcomes
cases.management: (1) Acknowledge grief - distinguish from 'abnormal' depression; (2) SSRI if severe (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - safe if considering further IVF; (3) Counseling with infertility specialist counselor; (4) Support groups for infertility (resolve India, local groups); (5) Address family pressure; (6) Open communication with husband; (7) Discuss options: further IVF, adoption, child-free living - without pressure; (8) CBT for infertility distress; (9) Address guilt and self-blame (male factor present); (10) Financial counseling for treatment costs; (11) Set boundaries with family; (12) Mindfulness for distress tolerance; (13) Coordinate with fertility specialist; (14) Consider break from treatment if needed

cases.presenting_complaint: Feeling 'numb', disconnected from self and body, alongside low mood
cases.associated: Emotional numbness, feeling like watching herself from outside, derealization, depersonalization, gaps in memory of recent events, identity confusion, difficulty feeling emotions (except sadness), self-harm historically (cutting), anhedonia, low mood, triggered by stress
cases.risk_factors: Complex trauma history (emotional abuse by mother, witnessed domestic violence), no previous treatment for trauma, recent work stress, recent anniversary of leaving abusive relationship, emotional invalidation in family of origin
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Somewhat detached, flat affect. Speech: Normal but emotionally distant. Mood: 'I just feel empty'. Affect: Depressed, notable emotional numbing. Thought: No psychosis, reports identity confusion. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Preserved, some memory gaps. Insight: Partial - knows she's dissociating but can't stop
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 16/27. DES-II (Dissociative Experiences Scale): 32/100 (elevated). No substance use. Rules out organic causes
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Self-harm history, chronic dissociation as emotion avoidance, passive SI during dissociation episodes. Risk increases when dissociative defenses fail
cases.explanation: This patient shows features of Dissociative Disorder (likely Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder) comorbid with Major Depression. Dissociation developed as protective mechanism against overwhelming emotions from childhood trauma. Depression has emerged/worsened likely because dissociative coping is failing under recent stress. Chronic dissociation (emotional numbing) prevents engagement with treatment and maintains depression. Treatment requires trauma-informed approach - dissociative symptoms may worsen with standard depression treatment initially. Need to stabilize before trauma processing
cases.management: (1) Safety planning given self-harm history; (2) Graded approach: stabilize dissociation first, then treat depression, then trauma processing; (3) SSRI (sertraline 50-100mg) - helps both depression and some dissociation; (4) Grounding techniques for dissociation episodes; (5) DBT for emotion regulation and distress tolerance; (6) Avoid premature trauma processing (can worsen dissociation); (7) Establish safe environment; (8) Develop distress tolerance skills; (9) Increase window of tolerance; (10) Address current work stress; (11) Trauma therapy once stabilized (EMDR or phase-oriented approach); (12) Long-term psychotherapy; (13) Family of origin work if appropriate; (14) Peer support for trauma survivors

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and worsening clutter in home over 5 years
cases.duration: Depression: 6 months. Hoarding: 5+ years, progressively worsening
cases.associated: Depression symptoms: Low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness. Hoarding symptoms: Extreme difficulty discarding possessions, cluttered home (only narrow pathways), acquisition of unneeded items (free stuff, sales), emotional attachment to objects, embarrassment about home, isolation due to not inviting people, some insight but unable to change, family conflicts about clutter
cases.risk_factors: Hoarding disorder (lifelong, worsened after retirement), previous depressive episodes, social isolation, retirement with loss of structure, no previous treatment for hoarding, perfectionism (decisions about discarding take hours), family history (mother hoarded)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed. Behavior: Talks rapidly about his 'collection', becomes defensive about clutter. Speech: Normal rate. Mood: 'Things just mean a lot to me'. Affect: Mildly depressed, some embarrassment about home. Thought: Preoccupation with possessions, some cognitive distortions (things might be needed, have value). Perception: No abnormality. cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 12/27. Hoarding Rating Scale: Severe. No cognitive impairment (MMSE 28/30). Rules out organic causes
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Distress related to hoarding, not depression severity
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depression and Hoarding Disorder. Hoarding disorder prevalence 2-6%, characterized by persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, resulting in clutter that impairs functioning. Depression often co-occurs - social isolation from hoarding leads to loneliness and low mood. This patient's hoarding worsened after retirement (loss of structure, purpose). Hoarding differs from collecting - involves clutter, discarding difficulty, and distress. Treatment requires addressing both conditions - CBT for hoarding is specialized (not standard depression CBT)
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (2) Specialized CBT for hoarding: cognitive restructuring about possessions, gradual discarding exposure, organizational skills; (3) Consider motivational interviewing for readiness to change; (4) Home visits by hoarding specialist if available; (5) Address perfectionism; (6) Develop decision-making skills; (7) Family involvement (without confrontation); (8) Social engagement despite clutter; (9) Address retirement loss; (10) Clean-up if safety hazard (fire risk, structural); (11) Consider professional organizer experienced with hoarding; (12) Long-term treatment - hoarding is chronic; (13) Set realistic goals; (14) Regular follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent low mood and fatigue despite sleeping 8+ hours nightly
cases.associated: Daytime sleepiness affecting work, loud snoring (partner complains), witnessed apneas (partner observed), morning headaches, difficulty concentrating, non-refreshing sleep, mood swings, reduced libido, depression affecting marriage, weight gain (15kg over 5 years)
cases.risk_factors: Obesity (BMI 32), neck circumference 17 inches, male sex, age 50+, alcohol use (worsens apnea), sedentary lifestyle, family history of sleep apnea, shift from active job to desk job 5 years ago
cases.mse: Appearance: Obese, appears tired. Behavior: Drowsy, slow. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Always exhausted, everything feels pointless'. Affect: Depressed, fatigued. Thought: No psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Reports poor concentration, memory. Insight: Partial - suspects sleep issues
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, testosterone low-normal. PHQ-9: 14/27. Epworth Sleepiness Scale: 16/24 (excessive daytime sleepiness). Overnight polysomnography: Moderate obstructive sleep apnea (AHI 22). ECG: Sinus rhythm with occasional ectopy
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Fatigue and mood likely secondary to sleep apnea
cases.explanation: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is strongly associated with depression - prevalence of depression in OSA patients is 20-40%, and treating OSA often improves mood. Proposed mechanisms: sleep fragmentation affecting neurotransmitters, hypoxia effects on brain, daytime sleepiness leading to inactivity and social withdrawal, and cardiovascular effects. This patient has moderate OSA with classic symptoms (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness). OSA is likely primary cause of depressive symptoms. CPAP treatment may resolve depression without antidepressant. OSA also explains concentration issues, headaches, and libido problems
cases.management: (1) Confirm OSA diagnosis with polysomnography (done); (2) FIRST-LINE: CPAP therapy - titrate pressure, educate on adherence; (3) Expect mood improvement over 4-8 weeks of CPAP use; (4) If depression persists after 4-6 weeks effective CPAP: add SSRI; (5) Weight loss program (15% weight loss can improve OSA); (6) Avoid alcohol (worsens apnea); (7) Sleep positioning (avoid supine); (8) Oral appliance if CPAP intolerant; (9) Address daytime sleepiness - no driving if severe; (10) Treat associated hypertension if present; (11) Follow-up sleep study after CPAP to confirm control; (12) Psychoeducation about OSA-depression link; (13) Monitor for residual depression; (14) Consider testosterone replacement if persistently low

cases.associated: Physical exhaustion from caregiving, emotional exhaustion, feelings of resentment toward mother, guilt about resentment, sleep disturbance (mother's night needs), reduced social life, no time for self, relationship strain (husband feels neglected), financial stress (reduced work hours), anhedonia, hopelessness

cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, ferritin low (iron deficiency). PHQ-9: 19/27. Zarit Burden Interview: 48/88 (severe burden). No organic illness causing symptoms

cases.explanation: Caregiver burden depression is common - prevalence 30-50% in caregivers of dementia patients. This patient shows classic caregiver burnout: emotional exhaustion, resentment, guilt, social isolation, and emerging depression. Cultural context (Indian daughter expected to care for parents) adds pressure. Caregiver depression worsens patient care quality. Resentment toward care recipient is common but guilt-inducing, creating cycle. This is NOT 'burnout' alone - clinical depression is present requiring treatment. Interventions must address both depression and caregiving situation
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (2) Assess and address caregiver burden; (3) Respite care - arrange regular breaks (essential for prevention); (4) Connect with caregiver support groups (local and online); (5) Discuss cultural expectations vs. practical needs; (6) Explore options: home health aide, day care for mother, family meeting about sharing care; (7) Psychoeducation about caregiver burnout; (8) Address guilt about resentment (normalize it); (9) Couples counseling for relationship strain; (10) Self-care planning (even small breaks); (11) CBT for coping strategies; (12) Financial counseling; (13) Advance care planning for mother; (14) Consider if caregiver can continue - alternatives if not sustainable; (15) Regular follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood with uncontrollable eating episodes for 6 months
cases.associated: Binge eating 4-5 times weekly (large amounts of food, loss of control), eating until uncomfortably full, eating when not hungry, eating alone due to shame, weight gain (12kg in 6 months), self-induced vomiting occasionally, mood worsens after binges, low self-esteem, avoidance of social eating, dietary restriction between binges leading to rebound binges
cases.risk_factors: History of childhood obesity, teasing about weight in school, family history of depression (mother), strict dieting in past, emotional eating patterns, recent job loss, social isolation, perfectionism
cases.appearance: Obese, appropriately dressed. Behavior: Shameful about eating, hesitant to discuss. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I hate myself for not being able to control eating'. Affect: Depressed, ashamed. Thought: Negative body image, 'I'm worthless', no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes binge eating but feels helpless
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, HbA1c 6.0% (prediabetic range), lipids elevated. PHQ-9: 17/27. Binge Eating Scale: Severe. Electrolytes normal (no purging to cause imbalance)
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. No active SI but low self-esteem, body image issues. Eating disorders have elevated suicide risk but binge eating lower than anorexia/bulimia
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Binge Eating Disorder (BED). BED prevalence 2-3%, characterized by recurrent binge eating without regular purging. Bidirectional relationship: depression can trigger emotional eating, and BED worsens depression through shame, weight gain, and isolation. Both share neurobiological mechanisms (reward dysregulation, impulse control issues). Treatment requires addressing both - SSRI helps both, psychotherapy for BED is specific (CBT-BED, interpersonal therapy). BED is distinct from bulimia (no purging) and obesity (BED involves loss of control episodes)
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - also reduces binge frequency; (2) Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is FDA-approved for moderate-severe BED; (3) CBT for BED (CBT-BED): psychoeducation, self-monitoring, cognitive restructuring, regular eating pattern, problem-solving; (4) Interpersonal therapy (IPT) for BED; (5) Address emotional eating triggers; (6) Avoid restrictive dieting (leads to rebound binges); (7) Regular eating schedule (3 meals + planned snacks); (8) Address body image; (9) Self-esteem work; (10) Weight management after binge control established; (11) Address job loss (precipitant); (12) Social support; (13) Long-term maintenance; (14) Monitor for type 2 diabetes development

cases.presenting_complaint: Hair pulling and low mood for 1 year
cases.associated: Hair pulling from scalp and eyebrows, increasing tension before pulling, relief after pulling, visible bald patches (hides with hair extension), attempts to stop but unsuccessful, social avoidance due to appearance anxiety, depression, shame, anxiety in social situations, affected academic performance
cases.risk_factors: History of trichotillomania since age 19, family history of OCD (cousin), perfectionism, anxiety tendency, stress at university, social anxiety secondary to hair pulling, no previous treatment for trichotillomania
cases.mse: Appearance: Hair extension used, appears anxious. Behavior: Reaches to hair during interview (caught herself twice). Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I'm so embarrassed, I look crazy'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Shame about appearance, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - knows pulling is harmful but can't stop
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 14/27. Trichotillomania Severity Scale: Moderate. No alopecia areata (dermatology confirmed). Iron studies: Ferritin low (may contribute to hair loss)
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Distress about appearance but good insight and treatment motivation
cases.explanation: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) is an OCD-related disorder characterized by recurrent hair pulling resulting in noticeable hair loss. Prevalence 1-2%. High comorbidity with depression (30-50%) - social avoidance and shame from visible hair loss lead to low mood. Trichotillomania often begins in adolescence (this case typical onset). Pulling is preceded by tension and followed by relief/pleasure - maintaining the behavior. Family history of OCD suggests shared neurobiological vulnerability. Treatment differs from depression alone - requires habit reversal training and SSRI at higher doses
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., fluoxetine 20-40mg) - higher doses may be needed; (2) CBT for trichotillomania: habit reversal training (awareness, competing response, social support), stimulus control; (3) Acceptable and Impact of Symptoms (AIS) therapy; (4) N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation - some evidence for impulse control; (5) Address iron deficiency (ferritin <30 associated with hair issues); (6) Cover strategies during university (scarves, wigs if needed); (7) Reduce social avoidance; (8) Address perfectionism; (9) Stress management; (10) Family involvement; (11) If refractory: consider clomipramine or N-acetylcysteine augmentation; (12) Long-term maintenance; (13) Coordinate with dermatologist

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and failure in college related to excessive gaming

cases.risk_factors: Gaming disorder (ICD-11 diagnosis), social anxiety (worsened by isolation), academic failure, limited real-world social skills, family conflict over gaming, personality traits (introverted, avoidant), peer group online only, recent failure causing depression
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, looks tired. Behavior: Anxious to return to gaming. Speech: Normal but minimal. Mood: 'What's the point, I'm a failure anyway'. Affect: Depressed, flat but animated when discussing gaming. Thought: Negative self-evaluation, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 15/27. Gaming Disorder assessment positive. Young Internet Addiction Scale: Severe. Sleep study: Delayed sleep phase disorder. No substance use

cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Gaming Disorder (now recognized in ICD-11). Bidirectional relationship: gaming provides escape from low mood but causes social isolation, sleep disruption, and academic failure that worsen depression. Gaming Disorder criteria met: impaired control, increasing priority, continuation despite harm. Treatment requires addressing both - depression with SSRI, gaming with behavioral intervention and social skills
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - may help anxiety too; (2) Address Gaming Disorder: gradual reduction, not cold turkey (causes distress); (3) Set structured gaming schedule; (4) Sleep hygiene and circadian rhythm normalization; (5) Academic counseling - address failed subjects; (6) Social skills training; (7) CBT for depression and maladaptive coping; (8) Address social anxiety; (9) Encourage real-world social activities; (10) Family therapy for conflict; (11) Consider residential program if severe; (12) Peer support (online gamers in recovery); (13) Future planning - career guidance; (14) Monitor for suicidality; (15) Long-term relapse prevention
